title: The Blaschka Object Network — M. Otto W. Möller Hamburg Forwarding Corridor
actor: M. Otto W. Möller / M. O. W. Möller, Hamburg
role: recurrent Hamburg forwarding intermediary in Robert Damon-mediated British and Irish orders
scope: Workshop-side evidence now shows a repeated Hamburg forwarding corridor across 1886–1887, not a one-off Liverpool handoff. Exact Möller wording occurs in the Galway/Cardiff, Dublin Museum, Marlborough and Liverpool sequences. A separate Haddon record has OCR 'M.Miller' and is retained as a probable but unverified occurrence. The register preserves case marks, invoices, prepayments, insurance where secure, onward recipients and failure/replacement evidence.
name_guard: OCR variants include N./M. Otto W. Moller, M. O'To W. Mollu, O.W. Müller and M. O. W. Moller. The recurrence of Hamburg, Damon, sequential case marks and the clean October 1887 form supports normalization to M. Otto W. Möller for the secure cluster. The Haddon record's shorter 'M.Miller' remains separately guarded. No modern Möller company is identified as successor without contemporary directory evidence.

events.date: early December 1887; exact day to be image-verified
events.onward_recipient: Higgins, Liverpool; exact name/title requires image and Liverpool-side verification
events.invoice: 268 Marks total stated in the dispatch letter
events.preceding_value_layers: A 23 November letter states that 247 Marks already prepaid for Liverpool covered the models only and asks for about 50 Marks more for packing. These remain distinct model-value, packing-estimate and later invoice/account layers.
events.payment_layer: The dispatch letter acknowledges a £25 draft, OCR-converted by a Dresden bank to 506 Reichsmarks, and carries remaining Damon credit forward toward Galway and Cardiff orders.
events.research_value: The Liverpool record places Möller inside a rolling Damon account that linked multiple institutional orders rather than treating each shipment as financially closed.

network_observation: Möller now emerges as a recurrent logistics node across Ireland, Wales and England. In January 1886 the same Hamburg intermediary handled Galway and Cardiff simultaneously; Dublin Museum instalments followed through the same node; Marlborough and Liverpool appear again in 1887. The workshop repeatedly bound case marks, invoice values, prepaid dealer balances and forwarding instructions together. The Dublin/Sollas failure adds a counterexample in which a shipper-note error changed the port, delayed the shipment and broke models. Missing case numbers are not reconstructed from sequence alone.
